title: Economy of Minds: Emerging Multi-Agent Intelligence with Economic Interactions
claim: A population of agents self-organizes over a task stream, with ineffective members eliminated and useful ones persisting, diversifying and connecting.
layout: 6 panels in a row along a labeled timeline arrow, with a legend underneath
description: A horizontal row of six rounded gray square panels sits above a long black timeline arrow labeled 'Stream of tasks'. A black triangle marker under each panel ties it to a point on the timeline. A trailing ellipsis after the last panel implies the process continues. Each panel is a small cloud of pastel circles (pink, green, purple, yellow, cyan, red) standing for agents. The population grows from 3 agents in the first panel to about 10 in the last. Thin black arrows between circles show topology links. Circles with bold black outlines mark newly created agents. Gray X marks mark eliminated agents. A legend below defines Agent, Creation, Elimination and Topology. The eye goes first to the timeline, then to the panels.
caption: Evolution of an agent society over a stream of tasks. Each panel shows the population at a given stage, where agents are continuously created, selected, connected, and eliminated. As the society encounters more tasks, ineffective agents are removed and corrected, while useful ones persist and diversify, leading to an alive and increasingly structured population.
abstract: How can a population of agents self-orchestrate and self-adapt into stronger collective intelligence without centralized control? Inspired by Friedrich Hayek's economic theory of decentralized coordination in markets, we study this question through an agent economy in which agents compete via auctions for the right to act, exchange payments, and accumulate wealth from environmental rewards. These simple local incentives induce decentralized credit assignment, driving global planning without explicit orchestration or communication protocols. The population evolves through economic selection: effective agents accumulate wealth and are mutated via exploitation, while ineffective ones go bankrupt and are replaced via exploration. Using modern Large Language Model (LLM) based agents, we show that, initialized with weak agents, the agent economy produces emergent multi-step reasoning strategies and outperforms stronger monolithic baselines across five agentic tasks, including mathematical reasoning, financial research, scientific research, accelerator design, and distributed-system optimization. Our results suggest a new path to multi-agent intelligence: rather than engineering coordination, we can design decentralized incentive structures under which it automatically emerges.
